Chapter 4: Navigating Anxiety and Self-Doubt
Anxiety—it's that quiet companion so many of us know all too well. Sometimes, it just hangs out in the background, and other times, it suddenly surges forward, catching you off guard. Picture this: your heart starts racing before a big meeting, you can’t sleep the night before a tough conversation, or you’re hit by that nagging feeling that something’s about to go wrong. And right alongside anxiety, there’s self-doubt, whispering in your ear that maybe you’re not ready, not good enough, not quite capable.
Let me tell you about a parent juggling work and family, who found herself wide awake at three in the morning. Her mind was spinning—replaying every mistake from the day, imagining worst-case scenarios, and wondering if she was failing the people who depended on her. In the darkness, every worry just felt bigger, almost overwhelming.
If you’re like most people, your first instinct might be to push anxiety away, to ignore it, or just power through. But here’s the thing: the more you fight it, the stronger it seems to get. That parent I mentioned? She discovered something simple but powerful—naming her fears. She started writing them down. Seeing those worries on paper made them feel less chaotic, less intimidating. Some of her fears were real, but a lot of them turned out to be just stories she was telling herself.
What she realized—and what’s so important—is that everyone deals with self-doubt at times. Even people who seem super confident on the outside have moments of uncertainty. The real trick isn’t to get rid of these feelings, but to figure out how to live with them.
She created small rituals to calm her mind: taking deep breaths, going for walks, reaching out to friends who really understood. Did these habits erase her anxiety? Not completely. But they helped her manage it, made it feel less overwhelming. And she learned the value of asking for help, of admitting when she was struggling.
Society often tells us that being strong means never showing weakness. But let’s be honest—real strength shows up when we’re honest with ourselves and others. When someone says, “I’m having a hard time,” it gives others a chance to step in—not to fix everything, but to listen and offer comfort.
The parent also started challenging her inner critic. When self-doubt crept in, she’d remind herself of the times she’d succeeded, the moments she’d overcome big challenges. She even kept a folder of kind notes from friends and colleagues, and she’d pull them out whenever she needed a little boost.
Most people don’t realize just how common these struggles really are. Sharing our experiences helps break the silence. And it’s such a relief to know you’re not alone—that others have faced the same feelings and found their way through.
